Implement a CloudWatch Events rule that invokes each function every 5 minutes to keep them warm.
Migrate all 15 functions to Amazon ECS Fargate tasks for consistent performance.

explanation: Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts by keeping pre-initialized execution environments ready. Application Auto Scaling with scheduled actions optimizes cost by reducing provisioned concurrency during low-traffic periods. Target tracking auto-scaling handles unexpected spikes. Option B (reserved concurrency) limits maximum concurrency but does not prevent cold starts. Option C (periodic invocations) is unreliable and wastes compute. Option D (ECS Fargate) introduces unnecessary complexity for simple Lambda functions.

stem: A company is designing a multi-tenant SaaS application where each tenant's data must be strictly isolated. Some tenants require dedicated infrastructure for compliance reasons, while others can share infrastructure to reduce costs. The application uses Amazon DynamoDB for data storage and Amazon ECS for compute. Which tenant isolation strategy should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Implement a tiered isolation model: Premium tenants get dedicated AWS accounts with their own DynamoDB tables and ECS clusters (silo model). Standard tenants share DynamoDB tables with tenant ID as the partition key prefix and use row-level security through IAM policies with dynamic condition keys. Use a central control plane to manage tenant provisioning and routing across both models.
Create separate DynamoDB tables for every tenant regardless of tier.
Use a single shared DynamoDB table for all tenants with application-level access control only.
Deploy all tenants in a single AWS account with separate VPCs for isolation.

explanation: A tiered isolation model balances compliance requirements (silo for premium tenants) with cost efficiency (pool for standard tenants). Dedicated accounts provide the strongest isolation for compliance-sensitive tenants. Shared tables with IAM-enforced row-level security provide cost-effective isolation for standard tenants. A control plane manages the complexity. Option B (separate tables for all) is expensive for thousands of tenants. Option C (application-only security) is insufficient for compliance. Option D (VPC-only isolation) does not isolate data at the storage layer.

stem: A company is migrating a legacy application that uses synchronous HTTP calls between 20 microservices. The tight coupling causes cascading failures when any service becomes unavailable. During migration to AWS, the architect wants to decouple the services to improve resilience. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Implement an event-driven architecture using Amazon EventBridge as the central event bus. Services publish domain events to EventBridge instead of making direct HTTP calls. For operations requiring responses, use the saga pattern with AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multi-service workflows with compensation logic for failures.
Replace all HTTP calls with Amazon SQS queues between every pair of services.
Add retry logic and circuit breakers to all existing HTTP calls using a service mesh.
Combine all 20 microservices back into a single monolithic application to eliminate inter-service calls.

explanation: EventBridge decouples services through event-driven communication, eliminating synchronous dependencies. The saga pattern with Step Functions handles multi-step workflows that previously relied on synchronous calls, with built-in compensation for failures. Option B (SQS between every pair) creates point-to-point coupling through queues. Option C (circuit breakers) improves resilience but does not decouple the services. Option D (monolith) reverses the microservices architecture.

stem: A company needs to implement a centralized cost allocation strategy across an AWS Organization with 150 accounts. Business units must see their own costs broken down by project, environment, and team. The finance team needs organization-wide cost visibility with the ability to forecast budgets and identify cost anomalies. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Implement a mandatory tagging policy using AWS Organizations tag policies for cost allocation tags (Project, Environment, Team). Enable AWS Cost Explorer with cost allocation tags activated. Configure AWS Budgets for each business unit with budget alerts. Enable AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to automatically identify unusual spending patterns. Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) exported to S3 for detailed analysis with Amazon QuickSight dashboards.
Use separate AWS accounts for each project to track costs by project.
Create IAM policies that prevent resources from being created without cost tags.
Use third-party cost management tools exclusively for cost visibility.

explanation: Tag policies enforce consistent cost allocation tagging across the organization. Cost Explorer with activated cost allocation tags provides self-service cost visibility per business unit. AWS Budgets with alerts enable proactive budget management. Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to identify unusual patterns. CUR with QuickSight provides detailed custom reporting. Option B (separate accounts per project) creates excessive account sprawl. Option C (IAM prevent creation) is too restrictive and blocks legitimate operations. Option D (third-party only) does not leverage native AWS cost management capabilities.

stem: A company operates a data pipeline that ingests 10 TB of data daily into Amazon S3, processes it with AWS Glue ETL jobs, and loads results into Amazon Redshift. The Glue jobs take 6 hours to complete and cost $500 per run. The company wants to reduce both processing time and cost. Which optimization should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks to process only new or changed data (incremental processing) instead of reprocessing the entire dataset. Switch from G.1X to G.2X workers for memory-intensive transformations. Enable Glue auto-scaling to dynamically adjust the number of workers based on workload. Convert output to Apache Parquet with Snappy compression for efficient Redshift loading.
Increase the number of Glue DPUs to the maximum to speed up processing.
Replace AWS Glue with Amazon EMR running Spark for lower cost per compute hour.
Schedule Glue jobs to run during off-peak hours for potential cost savings.

explanation: Job bookmarks eliminate reprocessing of already-processed data, dramatically reducing both time and cost. G.2X workers provide better performance for memory-intensive operations. Auto-scaling optimizes worker count dynamically. Parquet with Snappy compression reduces data volume and improves Redshift COPY performance. Option B (max DPUs) increases cost without addressing the root cause of reprocessing. Option C (EMR) requires operational overhead and may not be cheaper for this workload. Option D (off-peak scheduling) does not reduce processing time or cost.

stem: An e-commerce company needs to implement a product search feature that supports full-text search, faceted filtering (by category, price range, brand), fuzzy matching for typo tolerance, and autocomplete suggestions. The product catalog has 10 million items. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service with a dedicated search domain. Index product data with field-specific analyzers for full-text search. Use OpenSearch aggregations for faceted filtering. Configure fuzzy matching with edit distance for typo tolerance. Implement the suggest API with completion suggesters for autocomplete. Deploy in a Multi-AZ configuration with UltraWarm nodes for cost-effective storage of older product data.
Use Amazon DynamoDB with scan operations and client-side filtering for search.
Use Amazon CloudSearch for all search requirements.
Store products in Amazon RDS and use LIKE queries with wildcards for search.

explanation: OpenSearch provides purpose-built full-text search with analyzers, aggregations for faceted filtering, fuzzy matching for typos, and completion suggesters for autocomplete. Multi-AZ ensures high availability. UltraWarm reduces storage costs. Option B (DynamoDB scan) is extremely inefficient for search at scale. Option C (CloudSearch) has more limited features compared to OpenSearch. Option D (RDS LIKE queries) does not scale for full-text search with 10M items.

stem: A company is migrating a complex microservices application from on-premises Kubernetes to Amazon EKS. The application uses Istio service mesh for traffic management, mTLS, and observability. The team wants to maintain these capabilities on AWS while reducing operational overhead. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy Amazon EKS with AWS App Mesh as the service mesh replacement. App Mesh integrates natively with AWS services including X-Ray for distributed tracing, CloudWatch for metrics, and ACM for certificate management. Use App Mesh virtual gateways for ingress and traffic shifting for canary deployments.
Install the same Istio version on Amazon EKS and manage it manually.
Remove the service mesh entirely and use Application Load Balancers for all service-to-service communication.
Use Amazon API Gateway for all inter-service communication instead of a service mesh.

explanation: App Mesh is a managed service mesh that provides Istio-equivalent capabilities (traffic management, mTLS, observability) with AWS integration and reduced operational overhead. Native integration with X-Ray, CloudWatch, and ACM eliminates the need to manage separate observability and certificate infrastructure. Option B (manual Istio) maintains operational overhead. Option C (ALBs only) loses service mesh capabilities like mTLS, traffic splitting, and observability. Option D (API Gateway) is not designed for service mesh functionality.

stem: A company requires all inter-VPC traffic and internet-bound traffic to be inspected by a centralized security appliance. The company has 50 VPCs connected to AWS Transit Gateway. The security team wants inline traffic inspection without modifying application configurations in any VPC. Which architecture should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Create an inspection VPC with AWS Network Firewall deployed across multiple Availability Zones. Configure Transit Gateway route tables with a separate route table for the inspection VPC. Set default routes (0.0.0.0/0) in VPC route tables to point to Transit Gateway. Configure Transit Gateway route tables to route all traffic through the inspection VPC using appliance mode enabled on the Transit Gateway attachment to ensure symmetric traffic flow.
Deploy AWS WAF on all Application Load Balancers in each VPC for traffic inspection.
Use security groups and NACLs in each VPC to filter traffic without centralized inspection.
Install host-based firewalls on every EC2 instance across all 50 VPCs.

explanation: Network Firewall in an inspection VPC with Transit Gateway provides centralized inline inspection without application changes. Appliance mode on the TGW attachment ensures symmetric routing (both directions of a flow traverse the same firewall instance). Transit Gateway route tables direct all traffic through inspection. Option B (WAF) only inspects HTTP/HTTPS at the ALB level. Option C (SGs/NACLs) provide stateless/stateful filtering but not deep inspection. Option D (host-based firewalls) does not scale and requires per-instance management.

stem: A company uses Amazon CloudFront to serve a single-page application (SPA) from an S3 origin. After deploying updates, users report seeing stale content for hours. The CloudFront distribution has a default TTL of 86400 seconds (24 hours). The company deploys updates multiple times per day and needs users to see changes immediately without invalidating the entire distribution. How should the solutions architect solve this?

options.text: Implement asset fingerprinting by appending content hashes to static asset filenames (e.g., app.3f2a1b.js). Set long cache TTLs (1 year) for fingerprinted assets since the filename changes with every update. Set short TTL (60 seconds) or no-cache for index.html only, which references the fingerprinted asset filenames. This ensures browsers always get the latest index.html while benefiting from aggressive caching of static assets.
Set all CloudFront cache TTLs to 0 to disable caching entirely.
Create a CloudFront invalidation for all files after every deployment.
Use Lambda@Edge to add no-cache headers to all responses.

explanation: Asset fingerprinting is the standard solution for SPA cache management. Hashed filenames ensure updated assets get new URLs (and thus new cache entries), while index.html with a short TTL ensures users always get the latest version that references the current assets. Option B (disable caching) eliminates CloudFront's performance benefit. Option C (full invalidation) takes time to propagate and costs money at scale. Option D (no-cache for all) defeats the purpose of using a CDN.

stem: A company is building a document processing pipeline that must extract text, tables, and key-value pairs from millions of scanned PDF documents. The extracted data must be searchable and integrated with downstream business workflows. Documents range from 1 to 200 pages. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon Textract with asynchronous APIs (StartDocumentAnalysis) for large documents. Trigger processing via S3 events and Lambda. Use Textract's AnalyzeDocument with FeatureTypes including TABLES and FORMS for structured data extraction. Store extracted data in Amazon OpenSearch for full-text search and Amazon DynamoDB for structured key-value pairs. Use Amazon A2I (Augmented AI) for human review of low-confidence extractions.
Use Amazon Rekognition to extract text from PDF documents.
Build a custom OCR pipeline using Amazon SageMaker and Tesseract OCR.
Convert all PDFs to images and use Amazon Comprehend for text extraction.

explanation: Textract's async APIs handle large documents (up to 3000 pages). TABLES and FORMS feature types extract structured data. S3 events with Lambda provide scalable triggering. OpenSearch enables full-text search, DynamoDB stores structured data. A2I adds human review for low-confidence results. Option B (Rekognition) is for image analysis, not document text extraction. Option C (custom OCR) requires significant development and maintenance. Option D (Comprehend) is for NLP, not OCR/text extraction.

stem: A company is modernizing its batch processing system that currently runs on-premises using cron jobs and shell scripts to process files overnight. The system processes 10,000 files from various sources, applies transformation rules, and generates reports. The company wants a serverless, event-driven architecture on AWS. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon S3 event notifications to trigger AWS Step Functions workflows when files arrive. Step Functions orchestrates the processing pipeline: Lambda functions for lightweight transformations, AWS Batch with Fargate for compute-intensive operations, and Amazon SNS for completion notifications. Use S3 Lifecycle policies for processed file archival. EventBridge Scheduler replaces cron jobs for any time-based triggers.
Deploy the existing shell scripts on Amazon EC2 instances with cron jobs.
Use AWS Lambda functions triggered by CloudWatch Events on a schedule to poll for new files.
Migrate the batch processing scripts to AWS Glue jobs running on a schedule.

explanation: S3 events provide immediate, event-driven triggering without polling. Step Functions orchestrates complex multi-step workflows with error handling and retry logic. Lambda handles lightweight tasks while AWS Batch handles compute-intensive operations. EventBridge Scheduler provides serverless cron replacement. Option B (EC2 with cron) is not serverless and requires server management. Option C (Lambda polling) is wasteful and introduces delay. Option D (Glue only) is designed for ETL, not general batch processing.

stem: A company needs to enforce encryption at rest for all data stored across 200 AWS accounts in their organization. Different business units have varying encryption key management requirements: some must use customer-managed KMS keys, while others can use AWS-managed keys. No resources should be created with unencrypted storage. How should the solutions architect enforce this?

options.text: Create AWS Organizations SCPs that deny actions like s3:CreateBucket, rds:CreateDBInstance, ebs:CreateVolume, and similar resource creation actions unless encryption parameters are specified in the request. Deploy AWS Config organization rules with remediation actions to detect and auto-remediate any non-compliant resources. For business units requiring customer-managed keys, add SCP conditions that require the kms:ViaService condition with specific key ARN patterns.
Send monthly emails to account owners reminding them to enable encryption on all resources.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to check for unencrypted resources weekly.
Create IAM policies in each account that require encryption parameters on resource creation.

explanation: SCPs provide preventive controls that cannot be overridden by account-level permissions, ensuring encryption compliance organization-wide. Config organization rules provide detective controls with auto-remediation for any resources that bypass SCPs. SCP conditions with KMS key ARN patterns enforce customer-managed key requirements for specific OUs. Option B (emails) is not enforceable. Option C (Trusted Advisor) is detective only with delayed detection. Option D (IAM policies per account) can be overridden by account administrators.

stem: A company's Amazon RDS for MySQL database is experiencing connection exhaustion during peak hours. The database has a max_connections limit of 1000, but the application opens new connections for every request and does not reuse them. The application runs on Amazon ECS with 100 tasks. Which TWO solutions should the solutions architect implement? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the RDS instance. RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes database connections, reducing the number of connections to the database while handling thousands of application connections simultaneously.
Implement connection pooling in the application code using a library like HikariCP (Java) or SQLAlchemy connection pool (Python) to reuse connections within each ECS task.
Increase the RDS instance size to get a higher max_connections limit.
Create multiple read replicas to distribute connections across more database instances.
Switch to a database engine that supports unlimited connections.

explanation: RDS Proxy (Option A) multiplexes thousands of application connections into a smaller pool of database connections, directly solving connection exhaustion. Application-level connection pooling (Option B) prevents each request from creating a new connection, reducing connection creation overhead within each task. Together, they solve both the per-task and aggregate connection problems. Option C (bigger instance) only marginally increases max_connections. Option D (read replicas) only helps if queries can be split between read and write. Option E (unlimited connections) does not exist for production databases.

stem: A government agency needs to deploy a classified workload on AWS that requires data processing in an isolated environment with no internet access, no AWS service API access outside the isolated region, and hardware security module (HSM) backed encryption. Which AWS deployment model should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy on AWS GovCloud (US) Regions with a VPC that has no internet gateway, no NAT gateway, and uses VPC endpoints for required AWS services only. Use AWS CloudHSM clusters for encryption key management. Implement strict SCPs and IAM policies to prevent any data exfiltration. Use AWS PrivateLink for all service access.
Use standard AWS commercial Regions with enhanced security configurations.
Deploy on AWS Outposts for complete on-premises control.
Use AWS Local Zones for isolated, low-latency processing.

explanation: GovCloud provides isolated Regions designed for sensitive government workloads with FedRAMP High authorization. VPC without internet/NAT gateways plus VPC endpoints ensures no unauthorized external access. CloudHSM provides FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs for encryption. SCPs prevent cross-region or cross-account data movement. Option B (commercial Regions) may not meet government classification requirements. Option C (Outposts) does not provide the full range of AWS services. Option D (Local Zones) is for latency, not isolation.

stem: A company wants to decompose a monolithic Java application into microservices. The monolith has tightly coupled modules for user management, order processing, inventory, and payments. The team wants to minimize risk during decomposition. Which decomposition strategy should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Apply the strangler fig pattern: identify bounded contexts using domain-driven design (DDD). Extract one module at a time, starting with the least coupled module (e.g., user management). Deploy extracted microservices on Amazon ECS and route traffic using Amazon API Gateway. Keep the monolith running and gradually shift functionality using weighted routing. Use AWS App Mesh for service-to-service communication between the monolith and new microservices.
Rewrite all modules as microservices simultaneously and deploy them together.
Split the monolith by technical layers (UI, business logic, data) rather than by business domains.
Create a single Lambda function for each class in the monolith.

explanation: The strangler fig pattern enables incremental decomposition with minimal risk. DDD bounded contexts identify natural service boundaries. Starting with the least coupled module reduces integration complexity. API Gateway with weighted routing enables gradual traffic shifting. App Mesh manages communication between old and new components. Option B (simultaneous rewrite) is high-risk big-bang approach. Option C (technical layers) creates distributed monolith without business domain isolation. Option D (class-per-Lambda) creates thousands of nano-services with massive operational overhead.

stem: A financial institution must implement a disaster recovery strategy for their critical trading platform that requires an RPO of near-zero and an RTO of less than 1 minute. The platform uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, and Amazon ECS. The DR site must be in a different AWS Region. Which DR architecture should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Use Aurora Global Database with write forwarding enabled for near-zero RPO across Regions. Deploy an active-active ECS cluster in the DR Region behind a Global Accelerator endpoint. Use ElastiCache Global Datastore for cross-Region Redis replication. Configure Route 53 health checks with DNS failover to automatically route traffic to the DR Region within seconds of a primary Region failure.
Take hourly Aurora snapshots and copy them to the DR Region for recovery.
Use Aurora read replicas in the DR Region and promote manually during failover.
Replicate all data to the DR Region using AWS DMS with change data capture.

explanation: Aurora Global Database provides sub-second replication lag (near-zero RPO). Write forwarding allows the secondary Region to accept writes. ElastiCache Global Datastore replicates Redis data cross-Region. Active-active ECS eliminates RTO by having compute always running. Global Accelerator + Route 53 health checks automate failover within seconds. Option B (hourly snapshots) has RPO of up to 1 hour. Option C (manual promotion) exceeds 1-minute RTO. Option D (DMS CDC) adds replication lag and complexity.

stem: A company runs a serverless application using AWS Lambda with a total of 200 functions. The operations team struggles to troubleshoot issues because logs are scattered across individual Lambda function CloudWatch Log Groups, and there is no centralized way to trace requests that span multiple Lambda invocations. How should the solutions architect improve observability?

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing for all Lambda functions to provide distributed tracing across function invocations. Deploy Lambda Powertools for structured logging with correlation IDs that propagate across function calls. Create CloudWatch ServiceLens dashboards that combine X-Ray traces, CloudWatch metrics, and logs in a unified view. Use CloudWatch Contributor Insights to identify the top contributors to errors and latency.
Centralize all Lambda logs into a single CloudWatch Log Group using subscription filters.
Add custom print statements throughout the Lambda code for debugging.
Deploy a self-managed Elasticsearch cluster for log aggregation.

explanation: X-Ray provides distributed tracing showing request flow across multiple Lambda functions. Lambda Powertools adds structured logging with correlation IDs for request tracking. ServiceLens combines traces, metrics, and logs in one dashboard. Contributor Insights identifies error and latency patterns. Option B (single log group) centralizes logs but does not provide tracing or correlation. Option C (print statements) is unstructured and does not enable request tracing. Option D (self-managed Elasticsearch) adds operational overhead.

stem: A company is building an IoT platform that manages 5 million devices. Each device sends telemetry data every 10 seconds. The platform must support over-the-air (OTA) firmware updates, device shadow state management, and device-level access control. Which architecture should the solutions architect design?

options.text: Use AWS IoT Core with MQTT protocol for device communication. Implement IoT Device Shadow for state management, allowing applications to interact with devices even when offline. Use AWS IoT Jobs for managed OTA firmware deployments with staged rollouts and automatic rollback. Configure IoT policies with thing-level attributes for fine-grained device access control. Route telemetry to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time processing and Amazon S3 via Kinesis Data Firehose for long-term storage.
Use Amazon API Gateway with REST APIs for device communication and Amazon DynamoDB for device state.
Deploy MQTT brokers on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer.
Use Amazon SNS to push updates to devices and SQS to receive telemetry data.

explanation: IoT Core natively supports MQTT at scale for 5M devices. Device Shadow provides offline state management. IoT Jobs enables managed OTA updates with staged rollouts. IoT policies with thing attributes provide per-device access control. Kinesis handles the high-throughput telemetry (500K messages/second) for real-time and batch processing. Option B (API Gateway REST) does not support persistent device connections. Option C (self-managed MQTT) requires significant operational overhead. Option D (SNS/SQS) is not designed for bidirectional device communication.

stem: A company operates a multi-Region active-active application and needs to ensure that database writes in one Region are visible in the other Region within 1 second. The application uses a key-value data model with predictable access patterns. Users are routed to the nearest Region using Route 53 latency-based routing. Which database solution should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon DynamoDB global tables with multi-Region replication. DynamoDB global tables replicate data across Regions with sub-second latency and support multi-master writes, allowing both Regions to accept writes simultaneously. Use last-writer-wins conflict resolution for concurrent updates to the same item.
Use Amazon Aurora Global Database with write forwarding from the secondary Region.
Deploy Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with logical replication between Regions.
Use Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastore for all data storage needs.

explanation: DynamoDB global tables provide multi-Region, multi-master replication with sub-second consistency, matching the key-value data model and access pattern requirements. Both Regions accept writes simultaneously for true active-active operation. Option B (Aurora Global Database) typically has a single write Region (write forwarding adds latency). Option C (RDS logical replication) requires custom conflict resolution and has higher latency. Option D (ElastiCache) is an in-memory cache, not a primary data store.

stem: A company has an Amazon S3 bucket containing 100 TB of data partitioned by date (year/month/day). Amazon Athena queries against this data are slow because they scan the entire dataset even when queries filter by specific date ranges. How should the solutions architect optimize query performance?

options.text: Convert the data from CSV to Apache Parquet format with Snappy compression using AWS Glue ETL. Partition the data in S3 using Hive-style partitioning (s3://bucket/year=2024/month=01/day=15/). Register the partitions in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Enable partition projection in Athena to avoid partition metadata queries. This reduces data scanned by orders of magnitude for date-filtered queries.
Create an Athena workgroup with a higher query timeout to allow more time for scanning.
Move all data to a single large file to reduce the number of S3 GET requests.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to speed up data access from Athena.

explanation: Parquet with Snappy compression dramatically reduces data size (columnar format reads only needed columns). Hive-style partitioning with Glue Data Catalog enables Athena to scan only relevant date partitions. Partition projection further eliminates partition metadata lookup overhead. Together these optimizations can reduce data scanned by 90%+. Option B (longer timeout) does not reduce scan volume. Option C (single file) eliminates partition pruning. Option D (Transfer Acceleration) is for uploads, not Athena queries.

stem: A company is migrating a legacy application that uses a shared Oracle database accessed by 15 different applications. The company wants to move to a microservices architecture where each service owns its data. However, migrating all 15 applications simultaneously is not feasible. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Implement the database-per-service pattern incrementally. Start by identifying the least coupled application and migrating its tables to a dedicated Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL instance using AWS DMS with CDC for ongoing synchronization. Create a synchronization layer using DMS to keep the Oracle database and the new Aurora database in sync during the transition period. Repeat for each application, removing synchronization once all consumers are migrated.
Migrate the entire Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle and then split it later.
Create 15 copies of the Oracle database, one per application, and keep them synchronized.
Move the Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL in a single big-bang migration.

explanation: Incremental migration with DMS CDC maintains data consistency between the legacy Oracle database and new per-service databases during the transition. Starting with the least coupled application reduces risk. The synchronization layer ensures both old and new consumers see consistent data. Option B (RDS Oracle) does not achieve database-per-service. Option C (15 copies) creates massive data duplication and synchronization complexity. Option D (big-bang) is too risky for 15 applications.

stem: A company is building a serverless API that must handle unpredictable traffic ranging from 0 to 50,000 requests per second. The API performs CRUD operations on user profile data. The company wants to minimize operational overhead and cost during low-traffic periods while maintaining performance during spikes. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy Amazon API Gateway HTTP API (not REST API) with AWS Lambda proxy integration. Use Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity mode for the data layer. Enable Lambda provisioned concurrency with Application Auto Scaling for the most critical endpoints. Use API Gateway throttling and usage plans to protect downstream services from traffic overload.
Deploy an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS Fargate services.
Use Amazon API Gateway REST API with Amazon EC2 backends behind an Auto Scaling group.
Deploy Amazon CloudFront with Lambda@Edge functions for all API endpoints.

explanation: HTTP API offers lower latency and cost compared to REST API. Lambda scales automatically from 0 to thousands of concurrent executions. DynamoDB on-demand scales to handle any traffic without capacity planning and costs nothing when idle. Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts for critical paths. API Gateway throttling prevents downstream overload. Option B (ECS Fargate) has higher minimum cost than serverless. Option C (EC2) requires capacity management. Option D (Lambda@Edge) is designed for CDN customization, not full API backends.

stem: A company needs to provide temporary, elevated AWS access to on-call engineers during incidents. Normal access provides read-only permissions, but during an incident, engineers need administrative access to specific services for troubleshooting. Access must be time-limited, auditable, and require approval. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Implement a just-in-time (JIT) access solution using AWS IAM Identity Center with permission sets. Create an elevated permission set with the required administrative access. Use Identity Center's session duration to limit access time. Integrate with an approval workflow using AWS Step Functions and Amazon SNS for manager approval. CloudTrail logs all API calls made with the elevated permissions for audit purposes.
Share the root account credentials with on-call engineers during incidents.
Create permanent IAM users with administrative access for each on-call engineer.
Pre-assign administrative access to all engineers and rely on CloudTrail for auditing.

explanation: IAM Identity Center permission sets with session duration provide temporary, time-limited elevated access. Step Functions with SNS enables an approval workflow before access is granted. CloudTrail provides complete audit trail of all actions taken with elevated permissions. This implements the principle of least privilege with just-in-time access elevation. Option B (root credentials) is a severe security risk. Option C (permanent admin users) violates least privilege. Option D (pre-assigned admin) provides excessive standing privileges.

stem: A company uses AWS CloudFormation to manage infrastructure across 50 accounts. Template updates sometimes fail midway through stack updates, leaving stacks in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state. The team spends significant time manually fixing these failures. How should the solutions architect improve the deployment process?

options.text: Implement CloudFormation change sets for all updates. Review change sets before execution to identify potential issues. Enable stack termination protection for critical stacks. Use CloudFormation drift detection to identify manual changes that might cause update failures. Implement stack policies to prevent updates to critical resources. Use AWS CDK for infrastructure definition to benefit from type-safe constructs and built-in validation.
Delete and recreate stacks for every update instead of updating in place.
Stop using CloudFormation and manage all resources manually through the console.
Use a single large CloudFormation template for all resources across all accounts.

explanation: Change sets preview changes before execution, preventing unexpected modifications. Drift detection identifies manual changes that cause update conflicts. Stack policies protect critical resources from accidental modification. Termination protection prevents accidental stack deletion. CDK provides compile-time validation and higher-level abstractions that reduce template errors. Option B (delete/recreate) causes downtime and data loss. Option C (manual management) loses all IaC benefits. Option D (single template) exceeds CloudFormation limits and is unmaintainable.

stem: A company is migrating an on-premises application that uses a message-oriented middleware (MOM) based on IBM MQ for asynchronous communication between services. The application processes 10,000 messages per second with strict message ordering requirements per customer. Which AWS service should the solutions architect recommend as the target?

options.text: Use Amazon MQ with the ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ broker engine for protocol compatibility with existing JMS clients. Amazon MQ supports industry-standard messaging protocols (AMQP, STOMP, MQTT, OpenWire) for minimal code changes. For strict per-customer ordering, use message groups with the customer ID as the group identifier.
Use Amazon SQS Standard queues for maximum throughput.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with per-customer partition keys.
Use Amazon SNS for all message distribution between services.

explanation: Amazon MQ provides managed message brokers compatible with industry-standard protocols (JMS, AMQP, STOMP), minimizing code changes when migrating from IBM MQ. Message groups provide per-customer ordering. MQ handles 10K messages per second with broker scaling. Option B (SQS Standard) does not guarantee ordering. Option C (Kinesis) requires application changes from JMS protocol. Option D (SNS) is pub/sub, not a message queue replacement.

stem: A company needs to build a machine learning inference pipeline that processes 10,000 images per hour. Each image requires preprocessing (resizing, normalization), inference using a custom TensorFlow model, and post-processing (result aggregation, notification). The pipeline must be cost-effective and scale automatically. Which TWO components should the solutions architect include? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker serverless inference endpoints for the ML model serving. Serverless endpoints scale automatically from zero and charge only for compute time used, making them cost-effective for variable workloads.

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the pipeline: Lambda for preprocessing, SageMaker endpoint for inference, and Lambda for post-processing. Step Functions provides error handling, retry logic, and visual workflow monitoring.
Deploy the TensorFlow model on a continuously running p3.2xlarge EC2 GPU instance.
Process all images in a single Lambda function that loads the model on every invocation.
Use Amazon Elastic Transcoder for image preprocessing.

explanation: SageMaker serverless inference (Option A) provides auto-scaling ML inference that scales to zero when idle, optimizing cost for variable workloads. Step Functions (Option B) orchestrates the multi-step pipeline with built-in error handling and retry logic. Option C (always-on GPU) is expensive for 10K images/hour which may not need continuous compute. Option D (model loading per invocation) is extremely slow. Option E (Elastic Transcoder) is for video, not image preprocessing.

stem: A company with 500 developers across 10 teams needs to standardize their CI/CD pipelines while allowing teams flexibility in their build and deployment configurations. The company wants centralized governance over deployment targets, approval gates, and security scanning. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Create AWS CodePipeline templates using AWS Service Catalog. Define portfolio-level constraints that enforce mandatory stages (security scanning with Amazon CodeGuru, approval gates, deployment to specific accounts). Allow teams to customize build commands and test configurations within their Service Catalog product. Use AWS CodeBuild with shared custom Docker images for standardized build environments.
Create a single shared CodePipeline for all teams to use.
Let each team build their own CI/CD pipeline from scratch without standardization.
Use Jenkins deployed on EC2 instances managed by a central DevOps team.

explanation: Service Catalog provides standardized CodePipeline templates with mandatory stages (security scanning, approvals) while allowing team customization. Portfolio constraints enforce governance. Shared CodeBuild images ensure consistent build environments. CodeGuru provides automated code quality and security reviews. Option B (single pipeline) does not scale for 10 teams. Option C (no standardization) loses governance. Option D (Jenkins) requires infrastructure management and lacks native AWS integration.

stem: A company's Amazon Redshift cluster processes complex analytical queries that take 30-60 minutes. Users report that short dashboard queries (under 5 seconds normally) are slow when long-running queries are active. The cluster has 10 dc2.8xlarge nodes. How should the solutions architect resolve the query contention?

options.text: Enable Redshift Workload Management (WLM) with automatic WLM. Create separate query queues for short interactive queries and long-running analytical queries. Configure the short query queue with higher priority and concurrency. Enable Short Query Acceleration (SQA) to automatically route short queries to a dedicated processing pool, ensuring they complete quickly regardless of long-running query load.
Add more nodes to the Redshift cluster to increase overall capacity.
Schedule long-running queries to run only during off-peak hours.
Migrate all dashboard queries to Amazon Athena.

explanation: WLM with automatic management and SQA separates short and long-running queries into different processing pools. SQA automatically identifies and prioritizes short queries, ensuring they are not blocked by resource-intensive analytical queries. Priority-based queuing ensures interactive queries get resources first. Option B (more nodes) adds cost without solving the contention pattern. Option C (scheduling) delays analytical insights. Option D (Athena migration) requires significant dashboard changes.

stem: A company needs to migrate a Windows-based .NET application that uses Windows file shares (SMB) for document storage. The application is accessed by 200 concurrent users who share and collaborate on documents. The company wants to maintain the SMB interface while moving to AWS. Which storage solution should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with Multi-AZ deployment for high availability. FSx provides fully managed Windows file shares with native SMB protocol support, Active Directory integration, and DFS Namespaces compatibility. Configure daily automatic backups and enable shadow copies for user-accessible file versioning.
Use Amazon EFS with NFS protocol and configure the application to use NFS instead of SMB.
Deploy a Windows Server EC2 instance with an EBS volume configured as a file share.
Use Amazon S3 with AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway for SMB access.

explanation: FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed, native SMB file system with Windows ACLs, Active Directory integration, and DFS support. Multi-AZ provides high availability. Shadow copies enable user-initiated file recovery. This requires no application changes. Option B (EFS NFS) requires application changes from SMB to NFS. Option C (EC2 file share) requires infrastructure management and lacks high availability. Option D (Storage Gateway) adds latency and is better for hybrid scenarios.

stem: A company needs to build an event-sourced architecture for their financial transactions system. Every state change must be recorded as an immutable event. The system must support event replay, temporal queries (querying state at any point in time), and CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation). Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as the event log for ingesting transaction events with a 365-day retention period for replay capability. Store the canonical event log in Amazon DynamoDB with immutable records (no updates/deletes via IAM policy). For the read model (CQRS), use DynamoDB Streams to project events into Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL for complex temporal queries and Amazon ElastiCache for Redis for real-time read views.
Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with an events table and triggers for event processing.
Store all events in Amazon S3 and use Athena for temporal queries.
Use Amazon SQS for event storage with a 14-day retention period.

explanation: Kinesis provides ordered event ingestion with 365-day retention for replay. DynamoDB stores the immutable event log with IAM-enforced immutability. DynamoDB Streams projects events to read-optimized stores (CQRS pattern). Aurora PostgreSQL handles complex temporal queries. ElastiCache provides microsecond reads for current state views. Option B (RDS triggers) creates tight coupling and scaling issues. Option C (S3/Athena) has high latency for real-time queries. Option D (SQS 14-day) is insufficient for long-term event storage.

stem: A company is implementing a zero-trust network architecture on AWS. The security team requires that all network communication between services must be authenticated and encrypted, regardless of whether the services are in the same VPC. No implicit trust should be granted based on network location. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Deploy Amazon VPC Lattice for service-to-service communication. VPC Lattice provides built-in authentication and authorization using IAM policies and service network policies. All traffic is automatically encrypted using TLS. VPC Lattice works across VPCs and accounts without requiring VPC peering or Transit Gateway, and enforces identity-based access control at the network layer.
Use security groups to restrict traffic between services based on security group membership.
Implement mTLS manually using self-signed certificates on all application instances.
Deploy all services in private subnets and use NAT gateways for all communication.

explanation: VPC Lattice implements zero-trust principles with identity-based authentication (IAM), authorization policies, automatic TLS encryption, and cross-VPC/cross-account connectivity without network-level trust. Traffic is authenticated at the service level, not the network level. Option B (security groups) provides network-level trust based on group membership. Option C (manual mTLS) requires significant operational overhead for certificate management. Option D (private subnets) is network perimeter security, not zero-trust.

stem: A company runs a critical application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application requires exactly 30 seconds to gracefully shut down and drain existing connections. During scale-in events, instances are terminated before the application finishes draining, causing request failures. How should the solutions architect fix this?

options.text: Configure a lifecycle hook on the Auto Scaling group for the autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING event with a heartbeat timeout of 60 seconds. Update the application to call CompleteLifecycleAction when graceful shutdown is complete. This pauses the termination process, allowing the application to drain connections and complete in-flight requests before the instance is terminated.
Increase the Auto Scaling group cooldown period to 5 minutes.
Set the health check grace period to 60 seconds.
Disable scale-in events entirely to prevent termination.

explanation: Lifecycle hooks pause the instance termination, allowing the application to complete graceful shutdown (connection draining, finishing in-flight requests) before the instance is actually terminated. The heartbeat timeout of 60 seconds provides a buffer beyond the 30-second shutdown requirement. CompleteLifecycleAction allows early termination when shutdown is complete. Option B (cooldown) delays scaling actions but does not pause termination. Option C (health check grace) applies to newly launched instances, not terminating ones. Option D (disable scale-in) prevents cost optimization.

stem: A company is migrating a monolithic application that uses a relational database with 500 stored procedures containing complex business logic. The stored procedures handle data validation, business rule enforcement, and cross-table calculations. The company wants to move to a serverless architecture. How should the solutions architect handle the stored procedure migration?

options.text: Extract the business logic from stored procedures into AWS Lambda functions organized by business domain. Use Amazon API Gateway to expose the business logic as microservice APIs. Replace direct database calls with Lambda functions that validate data, enforce rules, and perform calculations before writing to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 PostgreSQL. Migrate incrementally using the strangler fig pattern.
Keep all stored procedures in the database and migrate to Amazon RDS for the same database engine.
Convert all stored procedures to database triggers in Amazon Aurora.
Rewrite all 500 stored procedures as a single Lambda function.

explanation: Extracting business logic into Lambda functions separates concerns and enables serverless scaling. Organizing by business domain creates natural microservice boundaries. API Gateway provides a service interface. Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute automatically. The strangler fig pattern enables incremental migration of 500 procedures without big-bang risk. Option B (keep in database) does not achieve serverless. Option C (triggers) maintains tight coupling to the database. Option D (single Lambda) creates a monolithic function that is hard to maintain.

stem: A company is designing a video streaming platform that must deliver live video with ultra-low latency (under 3 seconds) to 100,000 concurrent viewers globally. The platform must also support DVR-like functionality (pause, rewind, fast-forward on live streams). Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS Elemental MediaLive for live video encoding with multiple quality renditions. Use AWS Elemental MediaPackage for origin and packaging with time-shifted viewing (DVR) support. Distribute content through Amazon CloudFront with WebSocket-based low-latency streaming. Use AWS Elemental MediaStore for low-latency origin storage during live events.
Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams to ingest and serve live video to all viewers.
Deploy custom RTMP servers on EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer.
Record live streams to S3 and serve via CloudFront with a 30-second delay.

explanation: MediaLive provides real-time encoding with adaptive bitrate. MediaPackage provides just-in-time packaging with DVR/time-shifted viewing support. CloudFront with low-latency streaming achieves sub-3-second latency globally. MediaStore provides low-latency origin storage optimized for live video. Together they create an end-to-end managed live streaming platform. Option B (Kinesis Video) is for video analytics, not consumer streaming. Option C (custom RTMP) requires significant infrastructure management. Option D (S3 with delay) does not meet the latency requirement.

stem: A company needs to implement a data loss prevention (DLP) strategy across all S3 buckets in their AWS Organization. The strategy must automatically detect and protect sensitive data including PII, financial records, and healthcare information. Alerts must be generated when sensitive data is found in buckets without proper encryption or access controls. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie across all organization accounts using a delegated administrator. Configure Macie automated sensitive data discovery jobs to scan all S3 buckets for PII, financial data, and healthcare information using both managed and custom data identifiers. Create EventBridge rules to trigger Lambda-based remediation (enable encryption, tighten bucket policies) when Macie findings indicate sensitive data in non-compliant buckets.
Use S3 Object Lambda to scan every object for sensitive data when it is uploaded.
Implement AWS Config rules to check if S3 buckets contain sensitive data.
Manually review S3 bucket contents quarterly for sensitive data.

explanation: Macie provides ML-powered sensitive data discovery that automatically identifies PII, financial, and healthcare data in S3. Delegated administrator enables organization-wide coverage. EventBridge integration enables automated remediation. Custom data identifiers extend detection to company-specific sensitive data patterns. Option B (Object Lambda) adds latency to every read and does not scan existing data. Option C (Config) checks bucket configuration, not data content. Option D (manual review) does not scale and misses data between reviews.

stem: A company uses Amazon EKS and notices that application pods are frequently evicted due to node memory pressure. The pods do not have memory limits set, and some pods consume significantly more memory than expected, affecting other pods on the same node. How should the solutions architect prevent this?

options.text: Implement Kubernetes resource quotas and limit ranges at the namespace level. Set LimitRange objects that define default memory requests and limits for all pods. Configure ResourceQuota objects to cap total memory usage per namespace. Deploy the Kubernetes metrics server and configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale pods based on memory utilization instead of allowing unbounded growth.
Increase the node instance type to provide more memory per node.
Set all pods to run with Guaranteed QoS class by making requests equal to limits at the maximum possible value.
Disable memory-based eviction in the kubelet configuration.

explanation: LimitRange provides default and maximum memory limits for pods that do not specify their own, preventing unbounded memory consumption. ResourceQuota caps namespace-level usage. Metrics server and HPA enable memory-based scaling. These controls prevent a single pod from consuming all node memory. Option B (bigger nodes) delays the problem without solving it. Option C (max Guaranteed) wastes resources. Option D (disable eviction) causes node instability when memory is exhausted.

stem: A company is migrating a legacy application that processes sensitive financial data. The application currently runs on physical servers in a secure data center. The company must demonstrate to auditors that the migration to AWS maintains equivalent or better security controls. Which approach should the solutions architect use to satisfy audit requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Artifact to download AWS SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001 compliance reports demonstrating AWS infrastructure security. Map current on-premises security controls to AWS equivalent services using the AWS shared responsibility model. Deploy AWS Security Hub with the PCI DSS and CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark standards enabled. Use AWS Audit Manager to continuously assess AWS usage against compliance frameworks and generate audit-ready evidence.
Allow auditors to perform physical inspections of AWS data centers.
Provide auditors with root account access to verify security configurations.
Create a document listing all AWS services used without mapping to security controls.

explanation: AWS Artifact provides compliance reports accepted by auditors. Shared responsibility model mapping demonstrates control coverage. Security Hub with compliance standards provides continuous compliance monitoring. Audit Manager automates evidence collection and generates audit-ready reports mapped to compliance frameworks. Option B (physical inspection) is not available for AWS data centers. Option C (root access) is a security risk. Option D (service list) does not demonstrate control equivalence.

stem: A company needs to build a serverless data lake that ingests data from 50 different sources including databases, SaaS applications, and streaming sources. The data must be cataloged, transformed, and made available for self-service analytics by 200 business analysts. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS Glue crawlers to automatically discover and catalog data schemas from all sources into the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Use AWS Glue ETL jobs for data transformation and Amazon AppFlow for SaaS application data ingestion. Store all data in Amazon S3 with a raw/curated/published zone architecture. Enable AWS Lake Formation for fine-grained access control with tag-based permissions. Provide self-service analytics through Amazon Athena and Amazon QuickSight integrated with the Glue Data Catalog.
Load all data into Amazon Redshift as the central data warehouse.
Use Amazon EMR with Apache Hive for all data cataloging and transformation.
Store all data in Amazon DynamoDB and use PartiQL for analytics queries.

explanation: Glue crawlers auto-discover schemas from 50+ sources. AppFlow provides managed SaaS connectors. S3 zone architecture (raw/curated/published) organizes the data lake. Lake Formation provides centralized governance with tag-based access control for 200 analysts. Athena provides serverless SQL queries. QuickSight provides self-service visualization. Glue Data Catalog serves as the central metadata repository. Option B (Redshift only) is expensive for a full data lake. Option C (EMR Hive) requires cluster management. Option D (DynamoDB) is not designed for analytics.

stem: A company wants to enable cross-account access to Amazon S3 buckets without using bucket policies with wildcard principals. The company has strict security requirements that prohibit making buckets accessible to any AWS account not explicitly authorized. Which solution provides the most secure cross-account S3 access?

options.text: Use S3 Access Points with VPC-origin access point policies for each consuming account. Create a delegated access point in the consuming account that connects to the source bucket. Combine with S3 Block Public Access and bucket policies that only allow access through specific access points. Use AWS Organizations SCPs to restrict access point creation to authorized accounts only.
Create IAM roles with cross-account trust policies for S3 access.
Make the S3 buckets public and restrict access using CloudFront signed URLs.
Copy data between accounts using S3 replication rules.

explanation: S3 Access Points provide scoped, per-application access policies that are easier to manage than bucket policies. VPC-origin access points restrict access to specific VPCs. Delegated access points in consuming accounts reduce the need for complex bucket policies. Block Public Access prevents accidental exposure. SCPs restrict which accounts can create access points. Option B (IAM roles) is viable but harder to manage at scale. Option C (public buckets) violates security requirements. Option D (replication) duplicates data and increases cost.

stem: A company's Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster has grown to 10 TB. The company needs to perform a major schema migration that adds columns, changes data types, and creates new indexes. Traditional ALTER TABLE operations would lock the database for hours, causing unacceptable downtime. How should the solutions architect perform the schema migration?

options.text: Use the pt-online-schema-change (Percona Toolkit) or gh-ost tool for online schema migration. These tools create a shadow copy of the table, apply the schema changes to the copy, replicate data changes using triggers or binary log, and perform an atomic table swap. This allows the original table to remain fully operational during the migration with minimal locking.
Take an Aurora snapshot, restore it with the new schema, and switch traffic to the restored cluster.
Run ALTER TABLE during a maintenance window with the application in read-only mode.
Create a new Aurora cluster with the new schema and use DMS to migrate data.

explanation: Online schema change tools (pt-osc, gh-ost) perform schema migrations without blocking reads or writes. They work by creating a modified copy of the table and synchronizing changes in real-time, then performing a near-instantaneous table swap. This is the standard approach for zero-downtime schema changes on large MySQL tables. Option B (snapshot/restore) requires application cutover. Option C (maintenance window) causes hours of downtime on a 10 TB table. Option D (new cluster with DMS) is complex and requires cutover.

stem: A company is modernizing its application to use containers. The application consists of 30 microservices with varying compute requirements: some are CPU-intensive, some are memory-intensive, and some have GPU requirements for ML inference. The team wants to minimize infrastructure management. Which compute platform should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon EKS with a combination of Karpenter for automatic node provisioning and AWS Fargate for serverless pods. Karpenter automatically selects optimal instance types (CPU-optimized, memory-optimized, GPU) based on pod resource requirements. Use Fargate for batch and cron workloads that do not need persistent compute. Define node pools in Karpenter with different instance type constraints for GPU and non-GPU workloads.
Use Amazon ECS with a fixed set of EC2 instances and manual scaling.
Deploy all microservices on a single large EC2 instance type.
Use AWS Lambda for all 30 microservices regardless of compute requirements.

explanation: Karpenter automatically provisions optimal instance types (compute-optimized, memory-optimized, GPU) based on pod specifications, eliminating manual node management. Fargate provides serverless containers for batch/cron jobs. Node pools with constraints ensure GPU workloads get GPU instances. This combination minimizes infrastructure management while supporting diverse compute needs. Option B (fixed EC2) requires manual scaling and instance type management. Option C (single instance type) wastes resources. Option D (Lambda) cannot support GPU requirements and has runtime limits.

stem: A company needs to implement a global content management system (CMS) that serves content in 20 languages with regional content variations. Content editors in each region should be able to publish content independently. The system must handle 50,000 page views per second globally with sub-200ms response times. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use a headless CMS architecture with content stored in Amazon DynamoDB global tables for multi-Region writes. Serve content through Amazon CloudFront with Lambda@Edge for content assembly and language routing. Use Amazon S3 for static assets with CloudFront caching. Implement Amazon Translate for automated content translation with human review through Amazon A2I. Use DynamoDB Streams with Lambda to invalidate CloudFront cache when content is updated.
Deploy WordPress on a single EC2 instance behind CloudFront.
Use Amazon Lightsail to host a CMS application in a single Region.
Store all content in Amazon S3 as static HTML files and use CloudFront for distribution.

explanation: DynamoDB global tables enable regional content editors to publish independently with multi-master writes. CloudFront with Lambda@Edge provides sub-200ms response times globally. Lambda@Edge handles language routing and content assembly at the edge. Amazon Translate automates translation. DynamoDB Streams triggers cache invalidation for fresh content. Option B (single WordPress) cannot handle 50K pages/second or multi-Region editing. Option C (Lightsail) is not designed for global, high-traffic CMS. Option D (static S3) does not support dynamic content management by regional editors.

stem: A company needs to implement comprehensive logging and monitoring for a regulated environment. The regulations require that all infrastructure changes are tracked, all data access is audited, and all security events are correlated for threat analysis. Logs must be tamper-proof and retained for 10 years. Which THREE services should the solutions architect configure? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail with organization trail logging management events, data events (S3, Lambda, DynamoDB), and Insights events. Send logs to a centralized S3 bucket in a log archive account with S3 Object Lock (compliance mode) for tamper-proof 10-year retention.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty for threat detection across all accounts, correlating CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs using machine learning to identify security threats and anomalies.

Enable AWS Config with conformance packs for regulatory standards. Record all resource changes with Config rules for compliance checking. Enable Config aggregator for organization-wide visibility of infrastructure changes.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs with a 30-day retention period for all logs.
Deploy Splunk on EC2 instances for log aggregation and analysis.

explanation: CloudTrail (A) provides comprehensive API and data access logging with tamper-proof retention via S3 Object Lock. GuardDuty (B) correlates multiple log sources for threat detection. Config (C) tracks all infrastructure changes with compliance checking. Together they provide the required audit trail, threat analysis, and change tracking. Option D (CloudWatch 30-day) is insufficient for 10-year retention. Option E (self-managed Splunk) adds operational overhead and is not required with native AWS services.

stem: A company uses Amazon API Gateway REST APIs with Lambda integration. The API responses include large payloads (500 KB - 5 MB) of JSON data. Users report slow response times, especially on mobile networks. The company wants to reduce response sizes and improve API performance without changing the response data structure. How should the solutions architect optimize this?

options.text: Enable API Gateway payload compression by setting the minimumCompressionSize parameter. API Gateway automatically compresses responses using gzip when the client sends an Accept-Encoding: gzip header and the response exceeds the minimum size. This can reduce payload sizes by 70-90% for JSON data. Additionally, enable API Gateway edge-optimized endpoint type for CloudFront integration to serve responses from edge locations closer to users.
Split large responses into multiple smaller API calls using pagination.
Cache all API responses in ElastiCache to reduce response generation time.
Increase the Lambda function memory to generate responses faster.

explanation: API Gateway payload compression reduces JSON response sizes by 70-90%, dramatically improving transfer times on mobile networks. Edge-optimized endpoints route through CloudFront, reducing latency from edge locations. Both require no changes to response data structure. Option B (pagination) changes the data structure and requires client changes. Option C (ElastiCache) reduces backend time but not transfer time. Option D (more Lambda memory) reduces computation time but not transfer time.

stem: A company is migrating from a traditional three-tier web application (web servers, application servers, database servers) to AWS. The application serves 10,000 concurrent users during business hours and near-zero outside business hours. The company wants to optimize costs by scaling to zero when possible. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudFront for static content delivery. Deploy the web and application tiers on AWS App Runner, which automatically scales from zero to handle traffic and scales back to zero when idle. Use Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 for the database tier, which scales compute capacity automatically based on demand. This eliminates paying for idle resources outside business hours.
Deploy the application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of 2 instances.
Use Amazon Lightsail with fixed-size instances for predictable pricing.
Deploy on Amazon EKS with Fargate and set minimum replicas to 1.

explanation: App Runner provides a fully managed container platform that scales to zero, eliminating costs during off-hours. Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute capacity automatically, matching the traffic pattern. CloudFront caches static content at the edge. Together, the entire stack can scale to near-zero cost during off-hours. Option B (EC2 min 2) always runs at least 2 instances. Option C (Lightsail) has fixed costs regardless of usage. Option D (EKS min 1) always runs at least one pod and incurs EKS control plane costs.

stem: A company is building a real-time bidding (RTB) platform for digital advertising that must respond to bid requests within 100 milliseconds. The platform receives 500,000 bid requests per second at peak. Each bid decision requires looking up user profile data, campaign budget data, and historical click-through rates. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy the bidding engine on Amazon EC2 with placement groups (cluster) for lowest network latency between nodes. Store user profiles and campaign data in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled for microsecond lookups. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to log all bid events for real-time analytics. Pre-compute click-through rates using Amazon SageMaker batch transform and cache results in Redis.
Use AWS Lambda for the bidding engine to benefit from automatic scaling.
Use Amazon API Gateway with DynamoDB for all data lookups.
Deploy the bidding engine on Amazon ECS with Fargate for serverless containers.

explanation: EC2 with cluster placement groups provides the lowest possible network latency for the 100ms budget. ElastiCache Redis provides microsecond data lookups essential for the tight latency requirement. Kinesis handles 500K events/second for analytics. Pre-computed CTR models in Redis eliminate inference latency. Option B (Lambda) has cold start risk and may not meet 100ms consistently. Option C (API Gateway + DynamoDB) adds overhead with multiple service hops. Option D (Fargate) provides less network performance control than placement groups.

stem: A company is deploying AWS Landing Zone with multiple account types: sandbox, development, staging, production, and shared services. The company needs to establish network connectivity between all accounts while enforcing different security policies per account type. Sandbox accounts must have restricted internet access, and production accounts must route all traffic through a centralized inspection point. Which network architecture should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Deploy a hub-and-spoke network using AWS Transit Gateway with separate route tables per account type. Sandbox accounts use a route table that blocks internet access (no route to NAT/IGW). Production accounts use a route table that routes all traffic (0.0.0.0/0) through a centralized inspection VPC with AWS Network Firewall. Shared services accounts use a route table with direct access to all spoke VPCs. Use Transit Gateway flow logs for network monitoring.
Create individual VPC peering connections between all accounts.
Use a single Transit Gateway route table for all account types with identical routing.
Deploy separate internet gateways in each VPC and use NACLs for traffic filtering.

explanation: Transit Gateway with separate route tables per account type enables differentiated routing policies. Sandbox route tables exclude internet routes. Production route tables enforce inspection by routing through Network Firewall. Shared services get appropriate access. Flow logs provide auditing. This architecture scales as accounts are added. Option B (VPC peering) does not scale and lacks centralized routing control. Option C (single route table) cannot differentiate policies by account type. Option D (NACLs) provide basic filtering without centralized inspection.

stem: A company uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a complex data processing workflow with 20 Lambda functions. The workflow takes 3 hours to complete and processes financial data that must not be lost. Occasionally, individual Lambda functions fail due to transient errors, causing the entire workflow to restart from the beginning. How should the solutions architect improve the workflow resilience?

options.text: Implement Step Functions error handling with Retry and Catch blocks for each state. Configure exponential backoff retry policies for transient errors (Lambda.ServiceException, Lambda.TooManyRequestsException). Use Catch blocks to route persistent failures to an error-handling state that logs the failure and sends SNS notifications. Enable Step Functions execution event history logging to CloudWatch for debugging. For long-running workflows, use Express Workflows for sub-workflows and Standard Workflows for the main orchestration.
Add try-catch blocks inside each Lambda function to handle all errors silently.
Set the Lambda function timeout to the maximum (15 minutes) for all functions.
Use SQS queues between each Lambda function instead of Step Functions.

explanation: Step Functions Retry with exponential backoff automatically handles transient errors without restarting the entire workflow. Catch blocks route persistent failures to error handling. Execution history provides debugging context. Standard Workflows support long-running processes with built-in state persistence. Option B (silent catch) masks errors and may produce incorrect results. Option C (longer timeout) does not address transient failures. Option D (SQS queues) loses orchestration visibility and error handling coordination.

stem: A company is moving from a self-managed Kubernetes cluster on-premises to AWS. The cluster runs stateful applications including databases and message queues that use Kubernetes Persistent Volumes backed by local SSDs. The company needs to maintain persistent storage on AWS. Which storage solution should the solutions architect recommend for the EKS migration?

options.text: Use the Amazon EBS CSI driver for EKS Persistent Volumes requiring high-performance block storage (databases). Use io2 Block Express volumes for the most demanding workloads. For shared storage across pods, use the Amazon EFS CSI driver with EFS Access Points for multi-AZ persistent volumes. Install the AWS EBS Snapshot Controller for volume snapshots and backup.
Use EC2 instance store volumes for all persistent storage on EKS nodes.
Store all application data in Amazon S3 using the S3 CSI driver.
Use hostPath volumes mapped to EBS volumes attached to EKS nodes.

explanation: EBS CSI driver provides managed Persistent Volumes with different performance tiers (gp3, io2 Block Express) for databases. EFS CSI driver provides shared, multi-AZ persistent storage for pods that need ReadWriteMany access. Snapshot Controller enables backup via EBS snapshots. Option B (instance store) loses data when instances stop. Option C (S3) is object storage with high latency for database workloads. Option D (hostPath) ties pods to specific nodes and breaks scheduling flexibility.

stem: A company needs to build a compliance reporting system that tracks all changes to AWS resources across 100 accounts, determines if changes are compliant with corporate policies, and generates audit reports. The system must identify who made each change, when it was made, and whether it was authorized. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS Config with organization-wide aggregator to record all resource configuration changes. Deploy conformance packs with custom Config rules for corporate policy compliance checking. Use AWS Config advanced queries to search for non-compliant resources. Integrate with AWS CloudTrail to correlate resource changes with the IAM principal who made them. Generate compliance reports using AWS Audit Manager with custom frameworks mapped to corporate policies.
Write custom Lambda functions to poll all accounts for resource changes hourly.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to check for compliance across all accounts.
Deploy a third-party compliance tool on EC2 instances in each account.

explanation: Config records all resource changes with timeline history. Conformance packs apply custom compliance rules consistently. Config aggregator provides organization-wide visibility. CloudTrail correlation identifies who made changes. Audit Manager automates compliance reporting with custom frameworks. Advanced queries enable searching non-compliant resources. Option B (Lambda polling) misses changes between polls. Option C (Trusted Advisor) has limited compliance checks. Option D (per-account tools) creates operational overhead.

stem: A multinational company needs to implement a global identity strategy for 10,000 employees accessing AWS resources across 200 accounts. Employees are managed in Microsoft Active Directory on-premises. The company requires MFA, session duration limits, and attribute-based access control (ABAC) based on department and job title. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Deploy AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) integrated with the on-premises Active Directory via AWS Directory Service AD Connector. Configure SAML attribute mappings for department and job title. Create permission sets with ABAC policies using session tags derived from AD attributes. Enable MFA in IAM Identity Center. Set session duration limits on permission sets. Use automatic provisioning with SCIM to synchronize users and groups from AD.
Create IAM users in each of the 200 accounts for every employee.
Use Amazon Cognito user pools for employee authentication to AWS accounts.
Deploy Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) with individual SAML trust relationships to each account.

explanation: IAM Identity Center provides centralized SSO for all 200 accounts with AD integration. AD Connector connects to on-premises AD without replication. SAML attribute mappings enable ABAC using AD attributes (department, job title). Permission sets with session tags implement fine-grained ABAC. Built-in MFA and session duration limits meet security requirements. SCIM auto-provisioning keeps users synchronized. Option B (per-account IAM users) is unmanageable at scale. Option C (Cognito) is for customer identity, not employee SSO. Option D (AD FS per account) creates 200 trust relationships.

stem: A company uses Amazon SQS to queue jobs for processing by a fleet of EC2 worker instances. The average processing time per message is 5 minutes, but some messages take up to 30 minutes. Messages that take longer than the default visibility timeout (30 seconds) are being processed multiple times because they become visible again. How should the solutions architect fix this?

options.text: Set the SQS queue visibility timeout to 35 minutes (longer than the maximum processing time). Additionally, implement the ChangeMessageVisibility API call in the worker application to periodically extend the visibility timeout for messages that are still being processed.
