Create Config rules to detect non-compliant instances and trigger SNS alerts to account owners.
Send emails to account owners asking them to patch their instances within 48 hours.
Use AWS Inspector to patch instances automatically.
Create AMIs with patches and require all instances to be relaunched from new AMIs.

explanation: Patch Manager with Organizations integration provides centralized, automated patching across all 100 accounts. OS-specific patch baselines ensure appropriate patches. Maintenance windows automate the 48-hour timeline. State Manager ensures SSM agent health. Inventory tracks compliance. Config rules detect non-compliance. This scales to 5,000 instances without manual intervention. Option B (emails) relies on manual action and is not enforceable. Option C (Inspector) detects vulnerabilities but does not apply patches. Option D (AMI replacement) requires instance recreation and causes disruption.

stem: A company uses Amazon ElastiCache for Redis as a session store and cache for their web application. The Redis cluster occasionally experiences high CPU utilization (>90%) during peak hours, causing increased latency. Analysis shows that a small number of keys (top 100) receive 80% of all requests. How should the solutions architect optimize this?

options.text: Enable ElastiCache for Redis with reader replicas and configure the application to read from replicas for cache hits. Use ElastiCache for Redis cluster mode to distribute data across multiple shards. For the hot keys, implement client-side caching in the application with a short TTL to reduce Redis requests. Monitor hot keys using Redis SLOWLOG and CloudWatch ElastiCacheReplicationGroupId metrics. Consider using ElastiCache Serverless for automatic scaling.
Increase the Redis node instance type to a larger CPU class.
Add more shards to the Redis cluster for all keys.
Move the session store to DynamoDB and use Redis only for caching.

explanation: Reader replicas distribute read load across multiple nodes. Client-side caching for hot keys reduces Redis requests dramatically (80% reduction for 100 keys). Cluster mode distributes data across shards. SLOWLOG identifies performance bottlenecks. ElastiCache Serverless auto-scales based on demand. Option B (bigger instance) provides limited improvement for hot key patterns. Option C (more shards) may not help if hot keys land on the same shard. Option D (DynamoDB for sessions) adds latency compared to Redis.

stem: A company has 50 legacy applications running on Windows Server 2012 R2 which is approaching end of extended support. Some applications have compatibility issues with newer Windows versions. The company needs to migrate these applications to AWS quickly while resolving compatibility concerns. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) to migrate applications to EC2 instances. For applications compatible with newer Windows, migrate directly to Windows Server 2019/2022 instances. For applications with compatibility issues, use Windows Server 2019 with application compatibility tools. For applications requiring Windows Server 2012 R2, continue running on EC2 while planning modernization. Use AWS End-of-Support Migration Program (EMP) for Windows Server to package legacy Windows apps to run on newer Windows versions without code changes.
Remain on Windows Server 2012 R2 on-premises and accept the security risks.
Rewrite all 50 applications for Linux before migrating.
Use AWS Lambda to replace all Windows Server applications.

explanation: MGN provides automated lift-and-shift migration for quick migration. EMP for Windows Server packages legacy apps to run on newer OS versions without code changes, resolving compatibility issues. Running on EC2 provides time for modernization planning. This pragmatic approach handles the 50 applications with varying compatibility levels. Option B (remain on-premises) exposes the company to unpatched security vulnerabilities. Option C (rewrite for Linux) is too time-consuming for 50 applications. Option D (Lambda) cannot run Windows applications.

stem: A company needs to build an API that aggregates data from 10 different backend microservices into a single response for the mobile application. Currently, the mobile app makes 10 separate API calls, causing poor user experience due to latency. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend to reduce client-side complexity and latency?

options.text: Implement an API composition layer using AWS AppSync with GraphQL. Define a unified GraphQL schema that maps to all 10 backend services. Use AppSync resolvers to fetch data from each service in parallel. Clients make a single GraphQL query specifying exactly the fields they need, and AppSync aggregates responses from all 10 services into a single response. Use AppSync caching to reduce backend calls for frequently accessed data. Deploy pipeline resolvers for complex aggregation logic.
Create a single Lambda function that calls all 10 services sequentially.
Use API Gateway to proxy all 10 API calls from a single endpoint.
Have the mobile app continue making 10 separate calls in parallel.

explanation: AppSync with GraphQL provides a unified API that aggregates data from multiple backends. Parallel resolver execution minimizes latency. Clients request only needed fields, reducing payload size for mobile devices. Caching reduces backend load. Pipeline resolvers handle complex aggregation. Option B (sequential Lambda) adds latency by calling services one after another. Option C (API Gateway proxy) still requires the client to understand 10 endpoints. Option D (parallel mobile calls) maintains poor UX with multiple requests.

stem: A company is implementing a disaster recovery plan that requires RPO of 1 hour and RTO of 4 hours for their entire application stack (web tier on ECS, application tier on Lambda, database on Aurora, files on S3). The DR Region must be in a different continent. Which DR strategy should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Implement a warm standby DR strategy. Deploy Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in the DR Region (RPO < 1 second). Use S3 Cross-Region Replication for file data (RPO < 15 minutes). Pre-deploy the ECS cluster infrastructure in the DR Region using CloudFormation StackSets but keep task count at minimum. Store Lambda function code in both Regions. Use Route 53 health checks with failover routing to automatically redirect traffic. During failover, promote Aurora secondary to primary, scale up ECS task count, and Route 53 failover triggers automatically. This provides RPO < 1 hour and RTO < 4 hours.
Take daily backups and store them in the DR Region.
Deploy a full active-active architecture in both Regions.
Use AWS Backup to create cross-Region backups of all resources.

explanation: Warm standby provides the required RPO/RTO balance. Aurora Global Database replicates with sub-second lag (RPO). S3 CRR replicates files with minutes lag. Pre-deployed infrastructure with minimum capacity enables quick scale-up (RTO < 4 hours). Route 53 failover automates traffic redirection. This is cost-effective compared to active-active while meeting the requirements. Option B (daily backups) has RPO of up to 24 hours. Option C (active-active) exceeds the cost justified by 4-hour RTO. Option D (AWS Backup) has slower recovery times.

stem: A company runs a batch processing application on AWS that processes large datasets nightly. The application uses Amazon EMR with Spark jobs. The team finds that EMR cluster startup takes 15 minutes, and the cluster runs for only 2 hours before terminating. The 15-minute startup overhead is significant. How should the solutions architect reduce startup time?

options.text: Use Amazon EMR on EKS instead of standalone EMR clusters. EMR on EKS runs Spark jobs on existing EKS clusters, eliminating cluster provisioning overhead. Alternatively, use EMR Serverless which starts Spark jobs within seconds by pre-initializing compute capacity. EMR Serverless auto-scales based on the workload and scales to zero when the job is complete, eliminating both startup wait and idle compute costs.
Keep an EMR cluster running 24/7 to avoid startup delays.
Pre-create EMR clusters 30 minutes before the batch job runs.
Install Spark on EC2 instances and manage the cluster manually.

explanation: EMR Serverless eliminates cluster provisioning by pre-initializing compute. Jobs start within seconds and auto-scale. No idle compute costs when jobs are not running. EMR on EKS leverages existing Kubernetes clusters for faster job submission. Both options eliminate the 15-minute startup overhead. Option B (24/7 cluster) wastes 22 hours of compute daily. Option C (pre-creation) still has startup time, just shifted earlier. Option D (manual Spark) adds operational overhead.

stem: A company needs to build a platform for managing and deploying machine learning models in production. The platform must support model versioning, A/B testing of model versions, automatic rollback for degraded models, and model performance monitoring. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker Model Registry for model versioning and approval workflows. Deploy models using SageMaker endpoints with production variants for A/B testing (traffic splitting between model versions). Configure SageMaker Model Monitor to detect data drift and model quality degradation automatically. Set up CloudWatch alarms on Model Monitor metrics to trigger Lambda-based automatic rollback to the previous model version when performance degrades. Use SageMaker Pipelines to automate the model training, evaluation, and deployment workflow.
Deploy models on EC2 instances and manage versions through Git tags.
Use Lambda functions for model serving and S3 for model storage.
Deploy models in Docker containers on ECS without SageMaker.

explanation: SageMaker Model Registry provides versioned, auditable model management. Production variants enable A/B testing with configurable traffic splitting. Model Monitor detects data drift and quality issues. Automatic rollback via CloudWatch alarms prevents degraded model performance from impacting users. SageMaker Pipelines automates the ML lifecycle. Option B (EC2 with Git) lacks ML-specific features. Option C (Lambda) has model size and timeout limitations. Option D (ECS containers) lacks built-in model monitoring and A/B testing.

stem: A financial services company must implement a solution that prevents any AWS IAM user or role from performing actions that could lead to data exfiltration from their production environment. The specific concern is preventing users from copying data to personal S3 buckets, sharing AMIs publicly, or creating public-facing resources. Which comprehensive solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Create a comprehensive SCP that: denies s3:PutBucketPolicy and s3:PutBucketAcl actions that would make buckets public, denies ec2:ModifyImageAttribute that would share AMIs publicly, denies actions that create internet-facing resources (ec2:CreateInternetGateway in production), and requires s3:PutObject actions to target only organization-owned buckets using the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key. Enable S3 Block Public Access at the organization level. Deploy VPC endpoints and remove NAT gateways to prevent internet-based data exfiltration. Monitor with GuardDuty's S3 protection and CloudTrail data events.
Train employees on data handling policies and rely on compliance.
Block all internet access from all AWS accounts.
Encrypt all data with KMS keys that only production accounts can use.

explanation: The multi-layered approach prevents data exfiltration through SCPs (preventive), Block Public Access (preventive), VPC endpoints without internet (network-level prevention), and GuardDuty/CloudTrail (detective). The aws:ResourceOrgID condition ensures data can only be written to organization-owned buckets. This is comprehensive without being overly restrictive. Option B (training) does not provide technical controls. Option C (block all internet) prevents legitimate business operations. Option D (encryption) does not prevent authorized users from accessing and copying data.

stem: A company runs a high-availability application on Amazon EC2 across 3 Availability Zones. The application requires at least 6 instances to handle production traffic. Currently, the Auto Scaling group has min=6, max=12, desired=6 with 2 instances per AZ. If an AZ fails, only 4 instances remain, which is insufficient. How should the solutions architect ensure capacity during AZ failures?

options.text: Increase the Auto Scaling group minimum to 9 instances (3 per AZ). This ensures that if any single AZ fails, the remaining 2 AZs still have 6 instances (3+3), meeting the minimum capacity requirement. Configure the Auto Scaling group with AZ rebalancing to maintain even distribution. Use a capacity reservation in each AZ to guarantee instance availability during demand spikes. Set the maximum to 18 to allow scaling during peak traffic with AZ failure resilience.
Add a fourth Availability Zone to the Auto Scaling group.
Keep 6 instances but increase the instance size to compensate for failures.
Deploy additional instances manually when an AZ failure is detected.

explanation: Running 9 instances (3 per AZ) ensures N+1 AZ resilience: if one AZ fails, 6 instances remain across the other 2 AZs, meeting the minimum. AZ rebalancing maintains even distribution. Capacity reservations guarantee instances are available. The max of 18 allows double capacity during peak with AZ failure. Option B (4th AZ) still has the same problem if running minimum instances. Option C (bigger instances) reduces resilience to individual instance failures. Option D (manual deployment) introduces delay during failures.

stem: A company is modernizing an application that relies heavily on stored procedures in SQL Server. The application has 1,000 stored procedures that contain business logic, data validation, and reporting queries. The company wants to migrate from SQL Server to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL to reduce licensing costs. How should the solutions architect handle the stored procedure migration?

options.text: Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to automatically convert SQL Server stored procedures (T-SQL) to PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL. SCT converts approximately 80% of code automatically and flags the remaining 20% for manual review. Create an SCT assessment report to identify conversion complexity before migration. For procedures that cannot be auto-converted, use SCT's extension packs that implement SQL Server-specific functionality in PostgreSQL. Test all converted procedures using SCT data validation tools to ensure functional equivalence.
Manually rewrite all 1,000 stored procedures in PostgreSQL.
Keep SQL Server on RDS and migrate only the application code.
Remove all stored procedures and implement business logic in the application layer.

explanation: SCT automates the majority of T-SQL to PL/pgSQL conversion, dramatically reducing migration effort. Assessment reports help plan the migration timeline. Extension packs handle SQL Server-specific functions. Data validation ensures functional equivalence. Manual conversion is only needed for the ~20% that cannot be auto-converted. Option B (manual rewrite of 1,000) is extremely time-consuming and error-prone. Option C (keep SQL Server) does not reduce licensing costs. Option D (remove all) requires massive application refactoring.

stem: A company needs to build an intelligent document search system that allows employees to search across millions of documents stored in Amazon S3, Confluence, SharePoint, and ServiceNow. The search must understand natural language queries and return relevant passages, not just keyword matches. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon Kendra as the intelligent search engine. Configure Kendra data source connectors for S3, Confluence, SharePoint, and ServiceNow to automatically crawl and index documents. Kendra uses ML to understand natural language queries and returns passage-level answers extracted from relevant documents. Enable Kendra's FAQ functionality for common questions. Use Kendra access control to ensure employees only see documents they are authorized to access based on their corporate directory group membership. Integrate with Amazon Bedrock for generative AI-powered answer synthesis across multiple source documents.
Use Amazon OpenSearch to index all documents and implement keyword search.
Build a custom search engine using Amazon SageMaker with trained NLP models.
Use Amazon Athena to query document metadata stored in a Glue Data Catalog.

explanation: Kendra provides managed intelligent search with native connectors for S3, Confluence, SharePoint, and ServiceNow. ML-powered natural language understanding returns passage-level answers, not just document links. Access control integration ensures security. FAQ functionality handles common questions. Bedrock integration adds generative AI for synthesized answers. Option B (OpenSearch keyword) lacks natural language understanding. Option C (custom NLP) requires significant ML expertise. Option D (Athena) queries metadata, not document content.

stem: A company needs to implement a privileged access management (PAM) solution for their AWS infrastructure. System administrators should not have standing access to production resources. Access must be requested, approved, and automatically expire. All privileged sessions must be recorded. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Implement AWS IAM Identity Center with permission sets that provide elevated access. Create an access request workflow using Step Functions: administrators submit access requests, managers receive approval requests via SNS email, approved requests trigger a Lambda function that temporarily assigns the elevated permission set. Set session duration to 1 hour with automatic expiration. Use Systems Manager Session Manager for all interactive access, which records all session activity to S3 and CloudWatch Logs. CloudTrail logs all API actions taken during elevated access.
Give all administrators permanent administrative access and audit quarterly.
Use break-glass accounts with shared credentials for emergency access.
Deploy a third-party PAM solution on EC2 instances.

explanation: This implements zero-standing-privilege PAM using native AWS services. IAM Identity Center provides temporary elevated access. Step Functions and SNS automate the approval workflow. Lambda assigns and revokes access automatically. Session Manager records all interactive sessions. CloudTrail provides API-level audit. Automatic expiration ensures no lingering privileges. Option B (permanent admin) violates least privilege. Option C (shared credentials) lacks individual accountability. Option D (third-party PAM) adds cost and operational complexity.

stem: A company's AWS bill has increased 60% over the past year. The finance team cannot determine which teams or projects are driving the increase because resources are not consistently tagged and costs are spread across 100 accounts. How should the solutions architect implement cost visibility?

options.text: Enable AWS Cost Explorer with hourly granularity. Activate cost allocation tags for Team, Project, and Environment. Implement tag policies through AWS Organizations to enforce consistent tagging. Deploy AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) to S3 with hourly granularity. Build Amazon QuickSight dashboards connected to CUR data for detailed cost analysis by team, project, and service. Enable AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to alert on unexpected spending increases. Create AWS Budgets per team with SNS alert notifications at 80%, 100%, and 120% thresholds.
Review the monthly AWS bill summary and distribute costs equally among teams.
Create separate AWS accounts for every team and project.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to identify cost optimization opportunities.

explanation: Cost allocation tags enable attributing costs to teams and projects. Tag policies enforce consistent tagging. CUR provides the most detailed cost data. QuickSight dashboards provide self-service cost visibility. Cost Anomaly Detection catches unexpected increases. Budgets with alerts enable proactive spending management. Together these provide comprehensive cost visibility and control. Option B (equal distribution) does not reflect actual usage. Option C (account per project) creates excessive account sprawl. Option D (Trusted Advisor) identifies optimization but not cost attribution.

stem: A company is building a high-frequency trading platform that requires ultra-low latency data processing. The system must process market data feeds with sub-microsecond network latency between components, support kernel bypass networking for minimum overhead, and co-locate compute resources as close as possible to data sources. Which TWO AWS features should the solutions architect use? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances with Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) in a cluster placement group for the lowest possible network latency between instances. EFA provides OS-bypass capabilities for high-performance networking.

Use Amazon EC2 bare metal instances (e.g., c7gn.metal or c6in.metal) to eliminate hypervisor overhead and enable custom kernel networking stacks. Bare metal provides direct hardware access for kernel bypass networking using DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit) or custom network drivers.
Use AWS Lambda for processing market data feeds.
Use Amazon SQS for inter-component communication.
Deploy components on AWS Fargate for container-based processing.

explanation: EFA with cluster placement groups (Option A) provides the lowest possible inter-instance network latency with OS-bypass capabilities. Bare metal instances (Option B) eliminate hypervisor overhead and enable custom kernel networking (DPDK) for sub-microsecond packet processing. Together they provide the ultra-low latency required for HFT. Option C (Lambda) has cold start latency. Option D (SQS) adds milliseconds of latency. Option E (Fargate) has container networking overhead.

stem: A company is deploying a sensitive workload that must meet FedRAMP High compliance requirements. The workload processes Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). The company needs to ensure all AWS services used are FedRAMP authorized and that the deployment meets all technical controls. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Deploy the workload in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions which are authorized at FedRAMP High impact level. Use only AWS services that are within the FedRAMP High authorization boundary. Implement NIST 800-53 Rev 5 controls using AWS Config conformance packs for the NIST framework. Deploy AWS Security Hub with the NIST 800-53 standard enabled. Use AWS Audit Manager with the FedRAMP framework to continuously collect evidence and generate audit-ready reports. Encrypt all data with FIPS 140-2 validated cryptographic modules (AWS KMS with FIPS endpoints).
Deploy in standard AWS commercial Regions with enhanced IAM policies.
Use AWS Outposts for on-premises FedRAMP compliance.
Deploy in any AWS Region and rely on AWS's shared responsibility compliance.

explanation: GovCloud provides FedRAMP High authorized Regions for CUI. NIST 800-53 controls are the technical baseline for FedRAMP. Config conformance packs automate control validation. Security Hub with NIST standard provides continuous compliance monitoring. Audit Manager automates evidence collection for FedRAMP audits. FIPS 140-2 endpoints ensure compliant encryption. Option B (commercial Regions) may not meet FedRAMP High. Option C (Outposts) does not provide GovCloud isolation. Option D (any Region) does not ensure FedRAMP authorization.

stem: A company uses AWS Lambda functions that connect to resources in a VPC (Amazon RDS and ElastiCache). The Lambda functions experience cold start times of 10-15 seconds when they need to create new ENIs for VPC connectivity. How should the solutions architect reduce VPC-connected Lambda cold start times?

options.text: Lambda functions in VPCs now use Hyperplane ENIs, which are shared across function invocations and pre-warmed. Cold start times for VPC-connected Lambda have been reduced to under 1 second by AWS. To further optimize, ensure Lambda functions are configured with the minimum required VPC subnets and security groups. Use provisioned concurrency for the most latency-sensitive functions to eliminate cold starts entirely. Ensure the VPC subnets have sufficient available IP addresses for ENI creation.
Remove VPC configuration from Lambda functions and access RDS via public endpoints.
Deploy a NAT Gateway to speed up VPC networking for Lambda.
Increase Lambda function memory to reduce cold start time.

explanation: AWS's Hyperplane ENI improvements have reduced VPC-connected Lambda cold starts from 10-15 seconds to under 1 second. ENIs are now shared and pre-warmed. Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts entirely for critical functions. Sufficient subnet IP addresses prevent ENI creation delays. Option B (public endpoints) removes VPC security benefits. Option C (NAT Gateway) does not affect cold start time. Option D (more memory) does not significantly impact VPC cold start time.

stem: A company is migrating a legacy application that requires access to on-premises systems during and after migration. The application on AWS needs to communicate with on-premises databases, file servers, and internal APIs. The company requires encrypted, private connectivity with consistent performance. Which connectivity solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Establish AWS Direct Connect with a dedicated connection for consistent, low-latency private connectivity. Configure a Direct Connect gateway to connect to multiple VPCs across Regions. Set up a VPN backup connection over the internet for redundancy. Use Transit Gateway to connect the Direct Connect gateway to all VPCs. Configure BGP routing with failover to the VPN if Direct Connect fails. Use Direct Connect MACsec encryption for data in transit security on the physical layer.
Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN as the primary connection for all traffic.
Use public internet endpoints with TLS for all on-premises communication.
Deploy AWS Outposts in the data center for direct network connectivity.

explanation: Direct Connect provides dedicated, consistent performance with private connectivity to on-premises. Direct Connect gateway enables multi-VPC, multi-Region connectivity. VPN backup provides redundancy. Transit Gateway simplifies multi-VPC routing. BGP failover ensures automatic switchover. MACsec provides physical-layer encryption. Option B (VPN only) has variable performance and crosses the public internet. Option C (public internet) lacks consistent performance and private connectivity. Option D (Outposts) is for edge computing, not connectivity.

stem: A company is building a multi-player mobile game that requires real-time synchronization of game state across players with conflict resolution. Players may go offline and reconnect, requiring seamless state sync. The game has 1 million daily active users. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS AppSync for real-time game state synchronization via GraphQL subscriptions. Configure AppSync with DynamoDB as the data store and enable Delta Sync for offline support. When players go offline, AppSync stores mutations locally and synchronizes automatically on reconnect with server-side conflict resolution using Lambda functions. Use DynamoDB global tables for multi-Region support. Implement AppSync caching for frequently accessed game data. Use Amazon Cognito for player authentication.
Use WebSocket connections to EC2 instances for all game state communication.
Store game state in S3 and poll for changes every second.
Use Amazon SQS for game state message passing between players.

explanation: AppSync provides managed real-time synchronization via subscriptions. Delta Sync handles offline mutations and automatic reconnection sync. Lambda-based conflict resolution handles concurrent game state modifications. DynamoDB global tables provide multi-Region low-latency access. Cognito provides scalable player authentication. Option B (WebSocket on EC2) requires managing connection state and offline sync manually. Option C (S3 polling) has high latency and cost. Option D (SQS) is not designed for real-time multi-player sync.

stem: A company is implementing a comprehensive backup strategy for their AWS environment across 100 accounts. The strategy must include automated backups for EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, and S3. Backups must be encrypted, cross-Region copied for disaster recovery, and retained according to different policies (daily for 30 days, weekly for 1 year, monthly for 7 years). Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Deploy AWS Backup with organization-wide backup policies using AWS Organizations integration. Create backup plans with three rules matching the retention requirements (daily/30-day, weekly/1-year, monthly/7-year). Configure cross-Region copy rules for DR copies. Enable backup vault lock in compliance mode for immutable backups that cannot be deleted (required for 7-year retention). Use AWS Backup Audit Manager to verify backup compliance across all 100 accounts. Enable advanced features for EC2 application-consistent backups using VSS.
Write custom Lambda functions to take snapshots of each service on different schedules.
Use each service's native backup feature independently across all accounts.
Take manual backups monthly and store them in a central S3 bucket.

explanation: AWS Backup provides centralized, policy-driven backup management across all supported services and accounts. Organization policies ensure consistent backup coverage. Multiple retention rules handle different compliance requirements. Cross-Region copy provides DR protection. Backup vault lock ensures immutability for regulatory compliance. Audit Manager verifies backup compliance. Option B (custom Lambda) requires significant development and maintenance. Option C (service-native) lacks centralized management across 100 accounts. Option D (manual monthly) is insufficient and error-prone.

stem: A company runs a GraphQL API using AWS AppSync. The API has grown to serve 100,000 requests per second with complex nested queries. Some queries resolve to 10+ levels of nesting, causing backend timeouts and high latency. How should the solutions architect optimize the API performance?

options.text: Implement query depth limiting in AppSync to prevent excessively nested queries (set maximum depth to 5 levels). Enable AppSync caching with per-resolver TTL settings to cache frequently accessed data. Use AppSync pipeline resolvers to batch and optimize data fetching across nested levels. Implement DataLoader patterns in Lambda resolvers to batch and deduplicate database queries (N+1 query problem). Configure AppSync request throttling to protect backend services from query storms.
Increase the AppSync timeout to 30 seconds for complex queries.
Disable nested queries entirely in the GraphQL schema.
Add more DynamoDB read capacity to handle the query load.

explanation: Query depth limiting prevents pathological queries. Caching reduces backend load for repeated data. Pipeline resolvers optimize multi-step data fetching. DataLoader patterns solve the N+1 problem (fetching the same data multiple times in nested resolvers). Throttling protects backends. Together these optimizations dramatically improve GraphQL performance. Option B (longer timeout) masks the problem without solving it. Option C (disable nesting) removes legitimate API functionality. Option D (more DynamoDB RCU) helps with data layer but not resolver efficiency.

stem: A company has 10 TB of data in an on-premises Teradata data warehouse that needs to be migrated to Amazon Redshift. The data warehouse has complex views, macros, stored procedures, and BTEQ scripts specific to Teradata. Which migration approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to analyze the Teradata schema and convert views, macros, stored procedures, and BTEQ scripts to Redshift-compatible SQL. Generate an SCT migration assessment report to identify conversion complexity. Use SCT data extraction agents to migrate the 10 TB of data to Amazon S3, then load into Redshift using the COPY command with manifest files for parallel loading. Replace Teradata-specific SQL functions with Redshift equivalents using SCT's extension packs.
Manually rewrite all Teradata SQL for Redshift compatibility.
Use AWS DMS for the complete Teradata to Redshift migration including schema conversion.
Export Teradata data as CSV and import into Redshift using INSERT statements.

explanation: SCT provides automated conversion of Teradata-specific constructs (macros, BTEQ, stored procedures) to Redshift SQL. Assessment reports help plan the migration. SCT data extraction agents handle efficient 10 TB data migration via S3. COPY with manifests enables parallel loading. Extension packs bridge Teradata-specific functionality. Option B (manual rewrite) is extremely time-consuming. Option C (DMS alone) does not convert Teradata-specific SQL constructs. Option D (CSV INSERT) is extremely slow for 10 TB.

stem: A company is building a platform for managing and monitoring thousands of edge devices deployed in remote locations (oil rigs, wind farms, cell towers). Devices have intermittent connectivity and must process data locally for immediate decisions while synchronizing results when connected. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Deploy AWS IoT Greengrass on each edge device for local compute and ML inference. Greengrass enables Lambda functions and Docker containers to run locally on edge devices, processing data and making decisions without cloud connectivity. Use Greengrass stream manager to buffer and batch telemetry data for efficient transmission when connectivity is available. Configure IoT Greengrass local shadow service for device state management during disconnected periods. Use AWS IoT SiteWise Edge for industrial data processing at remote sites. Synchronize with AWS IoT Core when connectivity is restored.
Require all devices to have constant internet connectivity for cloud processing.
Deploy standalone Linux servers at each remote location running custom software.
Use satellite internet to ensure constant connectivity for all edge devices.

explanation: IoT Greengrass provides local compute, ML inference, and messaging that operates independently during disconnections. Stream manager handles data buffering and efficient transmission. Local shadows maintain device state offline. IoT SiteWise Edge processes industrial data locally. Everything synchronizes automatically when connectivity is restored. Option B (constant connectivity) is unreliable at remote sites. Option C (standalone servers) lacks managed updates and monitoring. Option D (satellite) is expensive and may still have interruptions.

stem: A company wants to implement infrastructure as code (IaC) governance across their AWS Organization. They need to ensure all infrastructure changes go through code review, are tested in a staging environment before production, and maintain an audit trail of who approved each change. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Store all CloudFormation/CDK templates in AWS CodeCommit with branch protection rules requiring code reviews. Use AWS CodePipeline for the deployment pipeline: CodeBuild runs cfn-lint and CloudFormation Guard for policy validation, deploys to staging via CloudFormation change sets (requiring manual approval), runs integration tests, then deploys to production with another manual approval gate. Use CloudFormation StackSets for multi-account deployment. CloudTrail and CodePipeline execution history provide the audit trail.
Allow developers to deploy CloudFormation directly from their local machines.
Use the AWS Console to create all infrastructure manually.
Store templates in S3 and deploy using CLI scripts without review.

explanation: CodeCommit with branch protection enforces code review. CodePipeline automates the deployment workflow with approval gates. cfn-lint and Guard validate templates. Change sets preview changes before execution. Staging deployment validates before production. Manual approval gates ensure human verification. StackSets handles multi-account deployment. CloudTrail provides complete audit trail. Option B (local deployment) bypasses reviews and testing. Option C (manual Console) has no audit trail or review process. Option D (S3 scripts) lacks governance controls.

stem: A company runs a critical application on Amazon ECS with rolling deployments. During deployments, the application experiences a brief period of mixed versions (old and new tasks running simultaneously) which causes compatibility issues with the shared database schema. How should the solutions architect eliminate mixed-version windows during deployments?

options.text: Switch from rolling deployments to ECS blue/green deployments using AWS CodeDeploy. Blue/green creates a complete new set of tasks (green) running the new version alongside the existing tasks (blue). Traffic switches atomically from blue to green once all green tasks pass health checks. There is never a mixed-version window because traffic switches to the new version all at once. Configure CodeDeploy with an AllAtOnce traffic routing configuration for instant switchover. Maintain the blue tasks for quick rollback if issues are detected.
Deploy database schema changes first and wait 24 hours before deploying application code.
Increase the minimum healthy percent to 100% in rolling deployments.
Schedule deployments during maintenance windows when no users are active.

explanation: Blue/green deployment eliminates the mixed-version window by running complete old and new versions simultaneously with atomic traffic switching. AllAtOnce routing ensures instant switchover with no period where both versions serve traffic. Blue tasks remain available for rapid rollback. Option B (delayed schema) still has mixed-version during the code deployment. Option C (100% min healthy) ensures old tasks remain but does not prevent mixed traffic. Option D (maintenance windows) does not eliminate the problem, just reduces impact.

stem: A company needs to build a real-time dashboard that visualizes operational metrics from 500 microservices. The dashboard must show request rates, error rates, latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), and dependency maps. It must update every 5 seconds. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Instrument all microservices with AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) to collect metrics, traces, and logs. Send metrics to Amazon CloudWatch with custom metric dimensions for per-service breakdowns. Use AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing and dependency map visualization. Deploy Amazon Managed Grafana connected to CloudWatch and X-Ray data sources for real-time dashboards with 5-second refresh. Use CloudWatch Metrics Insights for complex metric queries across services.
Build a custom monitoring system using DynamoDB and a React frontend.
Use Amazon QuickSight for operational dashboards with auto-refresh.
Deploy Prometheus and Grafana on EC2 instances for monitoring.

explanation: ADOT provides vendor-neutral instrumentation compatible with OpenTelemetry standards. CloudWatch stores metrics with custom dimensions. X-Ray provides distributed tracing with automatic dependency maps. Managed Grafana provides real-time dashboards with 5-second refresh and native CloudWatch/X-Ray integration. Metrics Insights enables complex cross-service queries. Option B (custom system) requires significant development. Option C (QuickSight) is for business analytics, not operational dashboards. Option D (self-managed Prometheus) requires infrastructure management.

stem: A company is modernizing a legacy application that uses synchronous, blocking I/O for all database and API calls. The application runs on a single large server and cannot scale horizontally because of in-memory session state and sequential processing. The company wants to achieve horizontal scalability on AWS. Which modernization approach should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Refactor the application to use asynchronous, non-blocking I/O patterns. Replace in-memory sessions with Amazon ElastiCache for Redis for externalized session management. Introduce Amazon SQS for decoupling synchronous workflows into asynchronous processing. Deploy the application on Amazon ECS with multiple tasks behind an Application Load Balancer. Use AWS Step Functions for orchestrating multi-step workflows that were previously synchronous. Implement circuit breaker patterns using AWS App Mesh for resilient service-to-service communication.
Deploy the application on a larger EC2 instance with more CPU and memory.
Use AWS Lambda to replace the entire application.
Add a read replica database to offload read queries.

explanation: Async I/O enables handling many concurrent requests per instance. Externalized sessions (Redis) enable horizontal scaling. SQS decouples synchronous workflows. ECS with ALB provides horizontal compute scaling. Step Functions replaces synchronous orchestration. Circuit breakers (App Mesh) prevent cascading failures. Together these enable true horizontal scalability. Option B (vertical scaling) has limits and does not fix the architecture. Option C (Lambda) may require significant rewriting for a blocking I/O application. Option D (read replica) only helps with database reads.

stem: A company has deployed Amazon GuardDuty across 300 accounts but receives too many low-severity findings that are false positives for their environment. The security team wants to reduce noise while ensuring high-severity findings are immediately actionable. How should the solutions architect optimize GuardDuty findings management?

options.text: Create GuardDuty suppression rules to automatically archive findings that match known false-positive patterns (e.g., expected traffic patterns, authorized penetration testing IPs). Configure GuardDuty finding filters in Security Hub to prioritize high and critical severity findings. Create EventBridge rules that match high-severity GuardDuty findings and trigger immediate Lambda-based automated remediation (isolate compromised instances, revoke compromised credentials). For medium findings, create EventBridge rules that create JIRA tickets for investigation. Provide feedback on false positives to improve GuardDuty's ML models.
Disable GuardDuty to eliminate all findings.
Increase the GuardDuty finding threshold to only show critical findings.
Process all findings manually without automation.

explanation: Suppression rules eliminate known false positives without disabling detection. Finding filters in Security Hub enable priority-based management. EventBridge with severity-based routing provides tiered response: automated remediation for high severity, ticket creation for medium. False positive feedback improves ML detection over time. Option B (disable) loses all threat detection. Option C (threshold increase) is not a GuardDuty feature. Option D (manual processing) does not scale for 300 accounts.

stem: A company's application uses Amazon DynamoDB with a Global Secondary Index (GSI) that is throttled during peak hours even though the main table has sufficient capacity. The GSI has a different partition key than the main table, and writes to the main table are causing the GSI to throttle because the GSI's write capacity is lower. How should the solutions architect resolve this?

options.text: Increase the GSI write capacity to match or exceed the main table's write capacity. DynamoDB writes to the GSI asynchronously, and GSI throttling causes back-pressure on the main table writes. Enable DynamoDB auto-scaling on the GSI with appropriate minimum and maximum capacity and a target utilization of 70%. Consider using on-demand capacity mode for both the table and GSI to eliminate capacity management entirely. Monitor GSI throttling using CloudWatch ThrottledRequests metric for the GSI.
Delete the GSI and use main table scans instead.
Create a second main table as an alternative to the GSI.
Reduce write traffic to the main table to prevent GSI throttling.

explanation: GSI throttling back-pressures main table writes. The GSI must have sufficient write capacity to handle the main table's write throughput. Auto-scaling with target tracking ensures the GSI scales with demand. On-demand mode eliminates capacity management entirely. CloudWatch monitoring enables proactive capacity management. Option B (delete GSI, use scans) is extremely expensive and slow. Option C (second table) requires application-level synchronization. Option D (reduce writes) limits application functionality.

stem: A company is building a platform for processing and delivering personalized email campaigns to 50 million subscribers. Emails must be personalized with recipient-specific content, sent at optimal times based on recipient timezone and engagement patterns, and tracked for opens, clicks, and bounces. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Amazon Pinpoint for campaign management, audience segmentation, and optimal send-time optimization. Configure Amazon SES for email delivery at scale with dedicated IP addresses for sender reputation management. Use Pinpoint journeys to create automated, personalized email workflows based on user behavior. Store subscriber profiles and engagement data in Amazon DynamoDB. Use Kinesis Data Firehose to stream Pinpoint engagement events (opens, clicks, bounces) to S3 for analytics. Build engagement dashboards with Amazon QuickSight.
Use Amazon SNS for sending emails to all 50 million subscribers.
Deploy a self-managed email server on EC2 instances.
Use Lambda functions to send emails one at a time via SES.

explanation: Pinpoint provides campaign management with audience segmentation, journey automation, and send-time optimization. SES handles high-volume email delivery with dedicated IPs for reputation management. Pinpoint journeys automate personalized workflows. DynamoDB stores subscriber data at scale. Kinesis Firehose streams engagement events for analytics. QuickSight provides engagement dashboards. Option B (SNS) is for notifications, not marketing emails. Option C (self-managed) requires managing sender reputation and infrastructure. Option D (Lambda per email) does not scale efficiently.
